newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu sets forex liberalisation goal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu sets forex liberalisation goal.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu set a one-year goal on Tuesday for liberalising Israel's foreign currency market and struggled to end a feud over the issue between the Treasury and the central bank.

A late night meeting on Monday between Netanyahu, Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Joseph Frenkel to try to settle the dispute stretched into early Tuesday, forcing Meridor to postpone a visit to the United States.
By 0400 GMT the three men had been meeting continuously for more than eight hours.
Frenkel has urged a rapid liberalisation process as well as a widening of the shekel's trading bands. Meridor opposes a widening of the bands and has sought a slower approach to liberalisation.

"The next stage in our liberalisation programme is in the foreign currency market and in fixing a timetable for the shekel to become fully convertible in world markets and in the direction of lifting most foreign currency controls," Netanyahu told a major Israeli economic conference on Monday.

"If I had to define our goal I would say that from about a year from now we would move from a situation in which everything is prohibited unless specified otherwise to a situation whereby everything is allowed except for a few specific and defined restrictions," he said.

Meridor told the conference, in the seaside resort of Caesarea, that the government's goal was to restart growth and that a widening of the bands would cause the shekel to appreciate, leading to a further slowing of the economy.
"The consequences would be more unemployment mainly in the most troubled areas, an increase in emigration and less immigration," Meridor said.
Israeli media reports said Meridor was likely to quit if Netanyahu rejected his position.

Apart from the dispute over economic policy, Israel Radio said Meridor and Netanyahu were at odds over how the decision was to be made. It said Netanyahu wanted to settle the matter now and that Meridor wanted the matter brought to the cabinet, where he felt sure he would prevail, for a decision.
Earlier at the conference Netanyahu said another budget cut must be made in addition to the seven billion shekel ($2.1 billion) reduction already made this year.
"The thing that must be done immediately is another fiscal cut. There is no escaping this," he said. He did not specify the size of the cut that was needed. ($1 = 3.41 shekels)
